items.title: Prompt caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai? Aur lambi chat idle chhodo to?
items.one_idea: Prompt caching only reuses the already-processed prompt prefix and never changes the answer; Claude Code now also compacts a very long idle chat before its one-hour cache expires so your next message does not reprocess everything.
items.spoken_hook: Prompt caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai?
items.hook_10s: AI interview mein pucha: caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai? Nahi, jawab bilkul same rehta hai. Isme teen baatein hain. [frame 0: two identical answer bubbles joined by an equals sign]
items.visual_idea: A prompt block is stamped 'processed' and kept in a box with a ticking clock; two answer bubbles with and without the box come out identical; near the end of the clock a long chat shrinks to a short card before the box closes.
items.everyday_anchor: You wait for a lift and the same chai order is remembered by the cafe so it is made faster, but it tastes the same.
items.example: Label example: a 200K token chat idle ~54 minutes gets compacted (release note); cache read 0.1x, 5-min write 1.25x (docs).
facts_to_verify: v2.1.299 (14 Oct 2026): 200K+ token chat idle ~54 min is compacted before its one-hour cache expires
Caching has no effect on output generation; response is identical
cache read 0.1x, 5-minute write 1.25x, default 5-min lifetime
Idle compaction is stated for the terminal (Claude Code CLI) only
items.cover_headline: Does prompt caching change the answer?
items.notes: Caveats: idle compaction is documented for the terminal only, do not generalize; release note says 54 min vs a one-hour cache while docs say default cache is 5 min (the 1-hour option is the one in play), explain or leave out; no savings percentage in sources, never claim one; do not say 'new' for caching itself. hook_type misconception_question is NOT yet allowed by validate_queue.py (see state/proposals/2026-10-17-misconception-question.md); validation fails on e101 until the owner approves.

items.title: Safety check crash hua, phir bhi AI ka kaam ho gaya: ab fail hone par block karo

facts_to_verify: v2.1.295 (8 Oct 2026) added onFailure: block for command and HTTP hooks

items.title: Context mein kya-kya jata hai? Context ke 5 sources
items.one_idea: The context is everything the model sees when it answers: system prompt, tools, examples, message history and external data, and each source should stay lean.
items.spoken_hook: Model ko jawab dene se pehle kya-kya dikhta hai?
items.hook_10s: Model ko jawab dene se pehle kya-kya dikhta hai? Ek window mein paanch cheezein. Aaj paanchon samajhte hain. [frame 0: an empty window frame with five labelled boxes outside]

facts_to_verify: context sources: system prompts, tools, examples, message history, external data
bloated tool sets and long histories are common failures; context is a finite resource

items.title: Context compaction kya hai? Lambi chat ko chhota kaise karte hain
items.one_idea: Compaction summarises a conversation that is nearing the window limit and restarts a new window with the summary, while low-risk pruning drops redundant tool outputs.
items.hook_10s: Context compaction kya hota hai? Lambi chat ko summary banakar chhota karna. Teen steps. [frame 0: a full window bar shrinking to a small summary card]
items.visual_idea: A filling window bar hits the limit, folds into a short summary card, and a fresh window opens holding only that card.
items.everyday_anchor: Packing a long WhatsApp group chat into a three-line summary for someone who just joined.
items.example: Label example: a 30-message chat compressed to a short summary.
facts_to_verify: compaction: summarising contents and reinitiating a new context window with the summary
low-risk pruning: discarding redundant tool outputs or messages
as context grows recall decreases (context rot)

items.title: RAG kya hai? AI ko apni notebook dekhne do
items.one_idea: RAG retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and adds it to the user's prompt, so the model answers from your documents.
items.hook_10s: RAG kya hai? AI jawab dene se pehle apni notebook se sahi pages nikalta hai. Teen steps. [frame 0: a question beside a shelf of notebook pages]
items.visual_idea: A question goes to a shelf of pages, the three closest pages light up, slide into the prompt box and then the answer appears.
items.everyday_anchor: Looking up the right page in your notes before answering an exam question.
items.example: Label example: a company handbook split into pages.
facts_to_verify: RAG pairs a pretrained language model with an external retrieval component (Lewis et al.)
RAG retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and appends it to the user's prompt
chunks turned into embeddings; most similar retrieved at runtime
items.notes: Caveat: q05/q17/q20 already cover RAG trade-offs and failures; this reel is the plain definition. The paper abstract does not measure provenance or knowledge updates, do not claim it did.

items.title: Interview: Poora PDF context mein daal doon ya RAG banaun?
items.one_idea: If a knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens you can put all of it in the prompt (with prompt caching); above that you retrieve chunks with RAG.
items.spoken_hook: 40 page का handbook, और उसने RAG बना दिया।
items.hook_10s: 40 page ka handbook, aur usne RAG bana diya. Use RAG ki zaroorat hi nahi thi. Interview mein yahi poocha jata hai. Teen rules. [frame 0: a small handbook beside a huge machine]

items.everyday_anchor: Carrying a thin notebook in your bag versus renting a whole library to read one chapter.
items.example: Label example: a 40-page handbook (illustrative, not a measured number).
facts_to_verify: under 200,000 tokens you can include the whole knowledge base in the prompt, RAG not needed
prompt caching cuts latency by more than 2x and costs by up to 90% (Anthropic's own figures)

items.title: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai? AI ki memory notebook
items.one_idea: The context window is a small, limited desk that gets cluttered as it fills; agent memory means writing notes to storage outside the window and reading them back when needed, and the memory tool is that notebook: a /memories folder your own app manages.
items.spoken_hook: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai?
items.hook_10s: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai? Kyunki uski desk chhoti hai. Notebook se yaad rakhta hai. Teen steps. [frame 0: a small desk crowded with papers beside an empty notebook]

items.everyday_anchor: You note an exam formula in your copy so you can clear your desk and find it again tomorrow.
items.example: Label example: a coding agent writes 'user prefers Python, project uses pytest' to a notes file and reads it next session.

items.title: How a model learns: forward pass, loss, gradient descent
items.one_idea: A model learns by guessing, measuring how wrong the guess was (the loss) and nudging its weight against the gradient, repeated until it converges; the same loop trains an LLM.
items.hook_source: the owner's own wording of 2026-10-19: the plain question, a 0.6 s pause, then the basketball analogy as the first teaching line (the filler 'kya use ratwaya jaata hai? Bilkul nahi!' between the hook and the start was cut by the owner)
items.visual_idea: A ball and hoop with four marks (shot, miss, understand, try again), then three cards hours to marks with one weight dial, a loss gauge, a loss curve with a dot sliding against the gradient arrow and a table of real runs, then the same run diverging with a larger step.
items.everyday_anchor: Learning basketball: take a shot, miss, understand the mistake, try again.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12): one weight w, marks = w x hours for 1, 2, 3 hours giving 2, 4, 6. Learning rate 0.1: w 1.867 and loss 0.083 after one update, w 2.0 after four. Learning rate 0.5: loss 18.667, 250.963, 3374.058 (diverges). Check question: marks 3, 6, 9 give w = 3.
facts_to_verify: Every number on screen is from the real run printed in docs-notes/pilot-script-day1.md section 6; the claim 'billions of parameters' is the largest models (more than 100 billion, GPT-3 175 billion).

items.title: Train, validation and test: three piles of data
items.one_idea: Data is split into three piles with three jobs: the model learns from train, validation is how we choose between models, and the test pile is opened once at the end, because only data the model has never seen says how it will do on new data.
items.spoken_hook: Train, validation aur test data alag kyun rakhte hain?
items.hook_source: the plain direct question (9 words), then the exam analogy as the first teaching line, no filler in between (owner's rule 8 of 2026-10-19)
items.visual_idea: A textbook, a mock test and a final exam become three piles; a grid of 1,000 dots is cut into three blocks of true size (70, 15, 15 percent); a model that memorises scores 100 on train and 72 on validation; a second model scores 82 on both and wins on validation; the test pile opens once and shows 79; peeking at the test score and changing the model turns the green pile gold.
items.everyday_anchor: Exam preparation: textbook practice, a mock test, then a final exam with questions you have never seen.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, seed 36, 1,000 fake points, 700 train, 150 validation, 150 test): model 1 copies the closest training point: train 100 percent, validation 72, test 71. Model 2 averages 151 neighbours (picked by validation among 1, 5, 15, 51, 151): train 82, validation 82, test 79. Median of 200 seeds: 100, 73, 72 and 81, 81, 79. The 1,000 emails are only the story; the script says the data is fake.
facts_to_verify: Training, validation and test sets and their jobs; repeated use of the test set makes the model fit it (Google ML Crash Course, fetched 2026-10-19). A model that only repeats the labels it has seen scores perfectly and fails on new data; tuning on the test set lets knowledge of it leak into the model (scikit-learn, fetched 2026-10-19). Every accuracy on screen is from the real run printed in docs-notes/pilot-script-day2.md.

items.title: Interview: Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao
items.one_idea: Top-K keeps a fixed count of the most probable next words, Top-P keeps the smallest set reaching a cumulative probability threshold, and Temperature reshapes the probability distribution.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ne poocha: LLM mein Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao.
items.hook_source: the owner's own script of 2026-10-19, used word for word
items.visual_idea: One next-word distribution for Aaj mausam bahut is cut at three for Top-K, accumulated to 90 percent for Top-P, and reshaped from sharp to flat for Temperature; NAMKEEN marks the tail.
items.example: EXAMPLE: a toy run with invented scores for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut' (state/runs/q105_toy_run.py, output in state/runs/q105_toy_run_output.txt): at T=1 ACHHA 36.7 %, GARAM 24.6 %, THANDA 16.5 %, NAMKEEN 0.6 %; top-k 3 leaves NAMKEEN out; top-p 0.9 keeps five words at T=1 and six at T=1.5; NAMKEEN is 0.015 % at T=0.5 and 1.874 % at T=1.5.
items.cover_headline: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P: what's the difference?
items.caption_note: Use the owner's command hook unchanged; one comment ask about NAMKEEN, with the answer not shown in the reel.
facts_to_verify: top_k: the number of highest probability vocabulary tokens kept for top-k filtering (Hugging Face GenerationConfig docs, fetched 2026-10-20)
top_p: only the smallest set of most probable tokens whose probabilities add up to top_p or higher are kept (same page)
temperature: the value used to modulate the next token probabilities (same page); sampling must be on (do_sample) for these to apply

items.title: Interview: Prompt mein examples dene se model hamesha behtar hota hai?
items.one_idea: Examples in a prompt show the model the shape of the answer and the allowed labels, so they usually help; but every example costs tokens on every request, a one-sided set or a bad order pulls the answer, and the only way to know is to measure with and without.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ne poocha: prompt mein examples dene se model hamesha behtar jawab deta hai?
items.hook_formula: interviewer_asked: one complete question of 11 words in plain words
items.hook_source: hook-writer interviewer_asked; the question passes the Question quality test (one sentence, 11 words, no stacked question, no jargon beyond 'prompt', 'examples', 'model')
items.visual_idea: The real classification prompt as a mono card under the hook from frame 0; it grows from 23 to 85 tokens when five examples are added (a real tiktoken count); two label chips feed a model box; three all-positive examples make a red ALWAYS POSITIVE? pill; a gauge from NEAR CHANCE to NEAR BEST swings with the examples and their order; three measuring runs (0, 3, 5 examples) on the same reviews.
items.everyday_anchor: Showing a new hire a few solved tickets before the real one: a good set teaches the format, a one-sided set teaches a bad habit.
items.example: EXAMPLE prompt (invented): 'Classify the review as positive or negative.' with up to five Review/Label pairs and the review 'The delivery was late and the box was damaged.' We ran tiktoken (o200k_base): 0 examples 23 tokens, 1 example 35, 3 examples 60, 5 examples 85; five examples add 62 tokens to every request, 62 million tokens over a million requests. No model result is shown or claimed.
facts_to_verify: Examples steer output format, tone and structure; they should be relevant and diverse so the model does not pick up unintended patterns; 3 to 5 examples (Anthropic prompting best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).

GPT-3 few-shot accuracy depends on the prompt format, the training examples and their order, from near chance to near state of the art; the model is biased toward answers near the end of the prompt or common in pre-training data (Zhao et al., 'Calibrate Before Use', abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Randomly replacing the labels in the demonstrations barely hurts performance across 12 models; the label space, the distribution of the input text and the overall format of the demonstrations matter (Min et al., abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Reasoning models often do not need few-shot examples: try zero shot first, then few shot if needed; examples must align closely with the instructions (OpenAI reasoning best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).
Token counts are from tiktoken o200k_base on the exact prompt shown; other models tokenize differently. API usage is billed per token (Anthropic pricing page, fetched 2026-10-19).
keywords: how many examples in a prompt
items.trap: Adding examples blindly. Reframed after reading the sources: labels barely matter (Min et al.), so the trap is not 'a wrong example is copied'; it is cost on every request, a one-sided or badly ordered set that pulls the answer, and never measuring against the no-example prompt.

items.title: Interview: Temperature, top-k aur top-p teeno laga diye. Output pe kaun sa asar karta hai?
items.one_idea: Temperature, top-k and top-p do three different jobs: top-k (by count) and top-p (by total chance) cut the list of next words, temperature only reshapes the chances of the words that are left, and changing one changes what another keeps.
items.spoken_hook: Chatbot ne bola: aaj mausam bahut namkin hai.
items.hook_source: the stake from frame 0 (the bot says something silly), then the interview question, then the answer first in one plain sentence (owner's rule 8 and his correction of 2026-10-19: no filler between the hook and the answer)
items.visual_idea: A chat where the bot says the weather is salty, then one toy list of 8 candidate words drawn as bars with their real chances (NAMKIN 0.6 percent); temperature 1.5 flattens the bars and makes NAMKIN three times likelier without removing it; a cut line after word 3 (top-k) removes it; a running total stops at 90 percent after 5 words (top-p); the same top-p keeps 6 words once the bars are flatter.
items.everyday_anchor: Choosing the next word like picking from a menu: top-k and top-p shorten the menu, temperature changes how strongly the menu favours the first items.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, invented logits for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut ...'): at T 1.0 ACHHA 36.7 percent and NAMKIN 0.6 percent; T 1.5 makes NAMKIN 1.9 percent (3.1 times) and removes nothing; top-k 3 keeps ACHHA, GARAM, THANDA (47.2, 31.6, 21.2 after renormalising) and NAMKIN is never drawn in 10,000 draws; top-p 0.9 adds 36.7, 61.4, 77.9, 88.9, 95.0 and keeps 5 words; T 0.5 gives ACHHA 56.3 percent, T 1.5 gives 28.8; top-p 0.9 keeps 5 words at T 1.0 and 6 words at T 1.5. Order of the stack in the run: temperature, then top-k, then top-p, then renormalise.
facts_to_verify: Anthropic Messages API reference (fetched 2026-10-19): temperature is the amount of randomness injected into the response (default 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0, closer to 0.0 for analytical tasks, closer to 1.0 for creative ones, not fully deterministic even at 0.0); top_k samples only from the top K options for each token to remove the long tail; top_p uses nucleus sampling: cumulative distribution in decreasing probability order, cut off once it reaches top_p. The same page marks all three as not settable on models released after Claude Opus 4.6 (not used in the reel).

Hugging Face 'How to generate text' (fetched 2026-10-19): lower temperature makes the softmax sharper; top-k keeps the K most likely next words and redistributes the probability mass among them; top-p picks from the smallest set of words whose cumulative probability exceeds p, so the set size changes with the distribution; top-p can be combined with top-k.

Holtzman et al., nucleus sampling (arXiv 1904.09751, fetched 2026-10-19): sampling from the dynamic nucleus of the distribution cuts the unreliable tail and avoids bland, repetitive likelihood-based text.

Every number on screen is from the seeded toy run in docs: toy_run.py (invented logits, labelled EXAMPLE); the claim 'top-p keeps more words when temperature is higher' is a result of that run and follows from flatter chances needing more words to reach p.
